concepts.title: Classification: Bringing Order to Raw Data

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Classification: Bringing Order to Raw Data' refers to.
questions.a: Raw data, collected unit by unit, is a jumble. Classification arranges it into homogeneous classes on some basis -- geographical, chronological, qualitative or quantitative -- so that the mass can be comprehended and subjected to statistical treatment.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Classification: Bringing Order to Raw Data'.
questions.a: Classification is sorting for sight -- one basis at a time, chaos becomes classes.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Classification: Bringing Order to Raw Data' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Variables, Frequency Distributions and Class Intervals

questions.q: Using the method 'Variables, Frequency Distributions and Class Intervals', work with: lower_limit = 200, upper_limit = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of class_mark.

Take the relation taught for 'Variables, Frequency Distributions and Class Intervals' and work with: lower_limit = 150, upper_limit = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of class_mark.
Explain in your own words what 'Variables, Frequency Distributions and Class Intervals' refers to.
questions.a: Quantitative data is organised by variables -- characteristics that take different numerical values. A frequency distribution records how many observations fall into each value or class interval; exclusive classes count values up to the upper limit, inclusive classes include both endpoints, and class marks stand for each interval.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Variables, Frequency Distributions and Class Intervals'.
questions.a: Count the cases per class -- the frequency distribution is the data's first portrait.

concepts.title: Loss of Information and Choice of Classes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Loss of Information and Choice of Classes' refers to.
questions.a: Grouping buys clarity at a price: individual values disappear into intervals, so some information is lost. The statistician must therefore choose the number and width of classes with care -- enough classes to preserve the pattern, few enough to stay readable.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Loss of Information and Choice of Classes'.
questions.a: Grouping trades detail for clarity -- the art is losing the least information for the most readability.
